newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico to have PRI "for very many years" -- leader.
newsitem.headline: Mexico to have PRI "for very many years" -- leader.

text.p: The Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI) has governed Mexico since 1929, and if Humberto Roque Villanueva has his way it will carry on ruling a good while longer.

Dismissing gloomy predictions, the leader of President Ernesto Zedillo's party predicted in an interview with Reuters on Monday that the PRI would chalk up another win in congressional and gubernatorial elections this July.
"There's going to be PRI for very many years to come," Roque said. "...a party which even in the worst conditions gets 35 percent of the votes is not a party which has any risk of disappearing."

To ensure the PRI wins, Roque and his men have deployed controversial tactics -- such as energetic campaigning by President Zedillo, who had promised to stay above the electoral fray in the interests of greater democracy -- and caricaturing the main opposition party leader as a Nazi.

Roque, a 53-year-old economist who previously served as leader of the PRI in the Chamber of Deputies, defended his party's campaign. "There's no dirty war. What there is is a different attitude ... of we PRI members who won't let things pass," Roque told Reuters.

"For eight years we have been putting up with the worst epithets, insults and arguments against us. Because we were the party in government it was considered for many years that we shouldn't reply. That has changed."

Roque accepted that the PRI party newspaper La Republica had caricatured Felipe Calderon Hinojosa, leader of the main conservative opposition party PAN, as a swastika-clad Nazi next to a picture of Hitler wearing a PAN armband but denied that this amounted to a smear.

"The National Action Party (PAN) doesn't want anyone to remember its origins," he said, adding that the PAN had favoured Mexican neutrality during the Second World War and wanted early recognition of Franco's fascist dictatorship in Spain.
"In politics, what you try to do is to give examples of the risks associated with authoritarianism, and for that you use caricatures, images or political reflections," he said.
"I don't think there is any offensive implication in the penal code or in the dictionary in the terms fascist, National Socialist, Falangist, communist, or PRI-ista. They are political definitions."
Roque also had harsh words for the main left-wing opposition, the Party of the Democratic Revolution (PRD).

The PRD was "a party of the violent" and its candidate for mayor of Mexico City, Cuauhtemoc Cardenas, reminded him of disgraced former Ecuadorean leader Abdala Bucaram because of the irresponsibility of his proposals, Roque said.
In July Mexico will elect a new lower chamber, a quarter of the Senate, six state governors and a mayor of Mexico City in what analysts expect to be the most closely contested vote ever.
Roque said his own internal polls, as well as published surveys done by others, pointed to the PRI keeping its majority in the lower house of Congress.

That will probably be thanks to a special electoral clause that allows a party an extra eight percent of representation in the chamber to guarantee a majority if it gains 43 percent of the national vote. "Our target (for the election) is a little higher but of course we have to be careful and our minimum prediction is to win 43 percent," Roque said.
PRI dominance in the Senate is guaranteed because only a quarter of that chamber is up for election and the PRI has a massive majority.
Roque insisted Zedillo's campaigning was "absolutely legal" and had proved highly popular with party militants. "It helps the electorate to see what is at stake," he said.
